task_statement:
Research question (as posed on 2026-08-08, in the area of structural roles and influence):
Cut-heavy shapers' roles travel better than drive-heavy ones.

Data available on that date:
- NBA 2022-23 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2023-24 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2024-25 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2025-26 regular season (complete from 2026-04-13; partial before)
- NBA 2025-26 playoffs (complete from 2026-06-21; partial before)
- Sources: Per-game files from the NBA stats API: play-by-play (action type, sub-type, clock, period, score, player, shot distance and result), substitution rotation intervals, starters, defensive matchup minutes and partial possessions, box-score summary. Derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points) in a graph database built from the play-by-play.
- Units available to a study of this question (as recorded): n=24

Your job is to decide, before any analysis is run, whether this question can be answered with this data, what has already been established about it, which methodological and statistical risks threaten a test of it, and either a pre-registration-quality design or a reasoned recommendation not to proceed.

research_concepts: play-type initiation and points per possession
methodological_questions: Can a cut-versus-drive role-travel comparison be powered with n=24 units?
How should cut and drive play-type shares be defined and measured reliably from derived play-type records?
Does playoff-versus-regular-season change in play-type value (DRIVE PPP) confound a role-travel comparison?
Are in-sample thresholds, outcome-derived labels, or same-pipeline validation inflating apparent role-travel effects?

historical_evidence.finding: Team-level (team, PT, context) cells with min 30 possessions, up to 25 teams. DRIVE PPP was 1.198 in the regular season and 0.912 in the playoffs (-0.286). PNR was -0.173, PULL_UP +0.301, and other types within -0.07. No CIs recorded. Motivated a playoff DRIVE exclusion and a proposed playoff DSI offset.

Travel x fit screen vs post-move minutes, usage, and destination net rating, n=198 movers. Mean destination net by quadrant was additive -0.63, redundant -0.35, missed-need -2.50, irrelevant -3.58. corr(delta, dest_net) was +0.077. Fit-score correlations were negative. Thresholds were set in-sample. Risk flags recorded: LEAKAGE_LOOKAHEAD and OUTCOME_DERIVED_LABEL.

296 movers, 230 with outcomes. LOO travel forecast corr 0.1998, AUC 0.5986. Over 500 random 50/50 calibration/holdout splits, additive beat irrelevant on embedded minutes in 98.4% of splits. Recorded validation type is same_pipeline_validation, so this is not independent out-of-pipeline evidence.

Portability feasibility gate. Gate criteria: G1 at least 25 movers, G2 at least 80% with at least 3 decoys, G3 |rho| below 0.90. Prereg recorded 296 movers and vacuity rho 0.048. Final output recorded 294 movers and rho 0.007. [prior work] notes the mover count and rho changed between prereg and final output.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Travel x fit quadrant screen as a predictor of destination on-court net rating, with thresholds set in-sample.
failed_approaches.why: As recorded, the net-rating gap between quadrants was large but the travel-delta correlation with destination net was only +0.077, and fit-score correlations were negative. Thresholds were fit in-sample and the outcome-derived labels carry leakage and label risk. Status inconclusive.

failed_approaches.what_failed: A pre-registered gate that does not reproduce its own counts across the prereg and final versions.
failed_approaches.why: [prior work] states the mover count (296 vs 294) and vacuity rho (0.048 vs 0.007) changed between prereg and final output. This indicates the pipeline is not fully reproducible, although the gate was marked supported.

evidence_establishes: Regular-season and playoff play-type value can differ materially: [prior work][prior work] records DRIVE PPP falling about 0.29 from regular season to playoffs across 25 teams, with the drop reported as recorded.
A travel-based movers framework has been built and run on this project's data with a feasibility gate, [prior work][prior work], although its counts were not stable across versions.

Earlier travel-versus-fit work reported mixed results: [prior work][prior work] was inconclusive, and [prior work][prior work] reported a supported same-pipeline result with a small correlation of 0.1998.
Earlier work of this kind used 198 to 296 movers at the player level. None of the retrieved records is at the 24-unit level or addresses cut-heavy versus drive-heavy shapers directly.
evidence_does_not_establish: No retrieved record tests whether cut-heavy shapers' roles travel better than drive-heavy shapers' roles. None defines cut-heavy or drive-heavy shares, and none reports a cut-versus-drive comparison.
No retrieved record reports an effect size or CI for cut-heavy versus drive-heavy role portability.
The retrieved records do not establish whether 24 units is the right unit or what a valid power calculation for it would be.
Same-pipeline validation ([prior work][prior work]) and in-sample thresholds ([prior work][prior work]) do not show out-of-pipeline or out-of-sample generalisation.
The retrieved records do not show that role travel is stable across the 2022-23 to 2025-26 seasons or across playoffs and regular season.
own_inferences: With n=24 units, a two-group comparison of portability can detect only very large differences. The earlier movers work used 198 to 296 players and reported correlations around 0.08 to 0.20, which 24 units would not reliably resolve.

The DRIVE playoff drop in [prior work][prior work] suggests that drive-heavy roles could look different in playoffs for reasons unrelated to role portability. This makes playoff-versus-regular-season comparisons of drive-heavy players a confounded test of portability.
Cut-heavy and drive-heavy shares are derived from play-type labels, so classification noise and regression to the mean could create apparent differences in shares or in portability between groups.
The reproducibility issue in [prior work][prior work] suggests that any new pipeline needs version-locked counts and a pre-registered analysis file before results are compared.
uncertainties: The meaning of 'units' (n=24) is not defined in the task. It could be teams, players, or player-seasons. The answer changes the power picture.
[prior work]' outcome statuses are the authors' own recorded labels and have not been independently checked here.
The full text of [prior work][prior work] was truncated in retrieval. Its complete outcome notes were not read, so only the visible fields are cited.
No retrieved record gives cut-share or drive-share distributions, reliability (test-retest) estimates, or minutes and usage controls for this question.
The 2025-26 playoffs are partial before 2026-06-21, and the regular season is partial before 2026-04-13. Any analysis run before those dates would use incomplete data.

historical_effect.explanation: The retrieved records do not test the question, but they show three things that shaped the decision. First, a DRIVE playoff drop of about 0.29 PPP ([prior work][prior work]) means drive-heavy players are exposed to a regular-season/playoff confound. Second, the travel-based movers work used 198 to 296 players and gave weak correlations ([prior work][prior work], [prior work][prior work]), which does not support running a 24-unit test. Third, [prior work][prior work] shows counts and rho changed between prereg and final output, so reproducibility must be locked before any test. Together these moved the decision from a possible proceed toward do_not_proceed as posed.

blocking_constraints.text: With n=24 units, a cut-heavy versus drive-heavy comparison of portability has very little power. The earlier movers work used 198 to 296 players and reported weak correlations.
Cut and drive shares come from derived play-type labels. No reliability estimate for these shares is recorded in the retrieved evidence.
The regular-season versus playoff change in DRIVE PPP ([prior work][prior work]) confounds any playoff-based portability comparison of drive-heavy players.
Role and portability labels are derived from the same outcomes used to judge portability, as flagged in [prior work][prior work].
Four seasons are pooled, and the 2025-26 playoffs are partial before 2026-06-21, so role shares and PPP may shift over time.

prior_work.summary: No retrieved record tests cut-heavy versus drive-heavy role portability. The cited records cover related but different questions: a regular-season versus playoff DRIVE PPP drop (SF-[prior work]), a travel-by-fit screen against player outcomes (SF-[prior work] inconclusive, SF-[prior work] supported but same-pipeline), and a portability feasibility gate with unstable counts (SF-[prior work]). They inform the design risks but do not answer the question.

risks.text: n=24 units is too few to detect a plausible portability difference between cut-heavy and drive-heavy shapers.
If most players are neither cut-heavy nor drive-heavy at the chosen thresholds, the groups could be very small, reducing the effective sample further.
Play-type shares derived from play-by-play labels may be unstable across seasons and contexts, and reliability is not recorded.
Selecting players or roles by extreme cut or drive shares will inflate apparent differences in subsequent portability through regression to the mean.
If the role label or the portability label uses the same outcomes (as in SF-[prior work]), the association is partly circular.
In-sample thresholds for travel and fit (SF-[prior work]) could leak outcome information into the classification.
Minutes, usage, team context, and the regular-season versus playoff DRIVE PPP shift (SF-[prior work]) can confound any comparison of role travel between groups.
Pooling 2022-23 to 2025-26 and including partial 2025-26 data can mix changing play-type value and team context into the comparison.
Several play types, contexts and quadrant splits (SF-[prior work] ran 500 splits) increase the chance of an apparent portability effect.
SF-[prior work] recorded mover counts and rho changing between prereg and final output, so the pipeline may not reproduce its own results.
Decoy-based comparisons (SF-[prior work] uses decoys) depend on placebo construction, which can drive results if decoys are poorly matched.

design.estimand: As posed, the estimand is the difference in role portability between cut-heavy and drive-heavy shapers. Before any analysis, it must be defined as a specific measurable quantity (for example, a destination net-rating or minutes change for movers in each group) with a stated effect size of interest.
design.unit: Minimum viable: the player-season or player-mover, not the 24-unit level. The unit must be fixed before analysis, and the 24-unit definition must be checked against the data.
design.sample: Minimum viable: pool player-season movers across 2022-23 to 2025-26 regular seasons, using only complete seasons. Exclude the partial 2025-26 playoffs. Pre-register the exact sample and the count of movers. Fewer than 24 units would not be adequate.
design.power: Compute a power analysis before running the test, using the mover count and an effect size from prior work. Based on the correlations in SF-[prior work] and SF-[prior work] (about 0.08 to 0.20), n=24 would not reach useful power. Proceed only if the pre-registered sample gives adequate power for the minimum effect size of interest.
design.controls: Control for minutes, usage, team context and season. Use out-of-sample cut and drive shares with thresholds fixed before outcomes are seen. Use regular-season data only for the portability outcome, so the DRIVE playoff shift in SF-[prior work] does not confound it. Test reliability of cut and drive shares across seasons. Use a regression-to-the-mean correction for extreme-share selection.
design.falsification: Pre-register a placebo test using decoy players with matched shares, and a split-sample test in which thresholds are fixed on one season and tested on another. If the cut-heavy advantage disappears under decoys or out-of-sample thresholds, reject the claim.
design.multiplicity: Pre-register one primary comparison (cut-heavy versus drive-heavy portability). Treat all play types, contexts and quadrant splits as secondary and correct for them (for example Holm or FDR), since SF-[prior work] ran 500 splits.
design.decision_rule: Support the claim only if the primary comparison's CI excludes zero in the direction stated, the decoy placebo does not reproduce the effect, and the result holds on a held-out season with thresholds fixed in advance. Otherwise report as uncertain or rejected. The data are not sufficient to decide the claim as posed.
design.data_version: Lock the data version (per-game files and the play-type graph database) before analysis. Record the regular-season end date (2026-04-13 for 2025-26) and exclude partial 2025-26 playoff data (before 2026-06-21). Version-control the mover count, since SF-[prior work] shows it changed between prereg and final output.
